title: Kemi Badenoch denies housing benefit cuts plan would make people homeless
description: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has denied her party's plans to cut housing benefit would make people homeless, but suggested some would have to "mo
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has denied her party's plans to cut housing benefit would make people homeless, but suggested some would have to "move somewhere cheaper".At Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, she had challenged Andy Burnham to commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying the cost could be covered by cuts to welfare.The Conservatives have claimed £4bn could be cut from the housing benefit bill, in part by allowing tenancies in areas where housing is expensive to come to an end.Asked whether she would be willing to make people homeless in order to fund defence, Badenoch told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the party would "protect existing tenants". During PMQs, Burnham argued national security "can't come at the expense of social security". He repeated that a target date for increasing defence spending to 3% of GDP would be announced in the spending review in the spring.The PM insisted he would get the welfare bill down in "the Labour way", by boosting council housebuilding, supporting young people into work and providing more mental health support.Badenoch said the government should cut housing benefit to fund defence spending now, adding she would exempt pensioners and existing tenants from the plans.Speaking on the Today programme, she said: "What we're doing is making sure that people are protected, but capping the amount that people get on benefits because we need to look after our national security."Without national security, there aren't going to be any benefits. We're all going to be in danger, far more people will be homeless, and the government's first duty is defence of the realm."Her proposed changes would be part of a package that would cut £23bn from welfare to partly fund an increase in defence spending. But Karen Buck, chairwoman of Generation Rent and a former Labour MP, said Badenoch's proposals would lead to "homelessness, temporary accommodation costs crippling local councils, renters in severe financial hardship".Housing benefit can be paid to people who are unemployed or on a low income to help cover the cost of rent. The amount someone can claim is linked to the Local Housing Allowance rate, which varies for different council areas.The number of people eligible to claim housing benefit has increased by more than one million since 2020, driven by the soaring cost of private rents.The total cost of housing benefit is forecast to hit £39bn this year, according to the Department for Work and Pensions, due to the increasing number of claimants.The Conservatives have set out how they plan to cut £4bn in total from the housing benefit bill, which they said would include a saving of at least £2.2bn from freezing social sector rents, by removing annual inflation-linked increases.Another £1.8bn would be saved by lowering Local Housing Allowance rates, which are based on private rental costs in the area, for new tenancies.For existing tenancies, rates would be frozen until they gradually fall in line.In an interview with BBC Breakfast, Badenoch was asked who would be affected by her plans to cut housing benefit.She said: "We have people who live in areas that are quite expensive and if people need local housing allowance they will need to move somewhere cheaper. "I think you should aspire to live wherever you want to live, but you shouldn't aspire for the government, i.e. other taxpayers, to pay for you to live wherever you want to live..."We're not removing people from homes - this doesn't cover pensioners, it doesn't affect existing tenants - but I do think you need to be fair."Responding to Badenoch at PMQs, Burnham had said the policy would worsen homelessness and end up costing the government more.He said: "I don't think, myself, that taking £4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation."

schema.headline: Kemi Badenoch denies housing benefit cuts plan would make people homeless

title: Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches
description: Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found,
body: Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found, escalating its use of a weapon that Kyiv's air defences are struggling to deal with.It marked the first time that daily attacks by Moscow's new upgraded Geran drones were recorded in Ukrainian Air Force data. The growing use of jet-propelled and other varieties of drones prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to condemn what he called an unfolding "horror" over the skies of Kyiv.Ukraine's military recently told the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks grew from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. In five of the nightly attacks in August, these drones outnumbered the older, slower models."The reason for turning to jet-powered drones is that they are much faster than the previous generation and it makes it much more difficult for Ukraine to intercept them," said Dr Marina Miron, an expert on military technology at King's College London.The upgraded munitions can cruise at more than 300mph, significantly faster than older models and well beyond the top speed of Kyiv's interceptors. The drones are powered by turbojet engines, some of which, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, are sourced from China.According to Zelensky, the drones were used as part of a wave of attacks that killed at least 12 people and injured 20 more on 1 September. Six of the casualties were railway workers after a depot was hit in Kyiv.And on Wednesday the Moldovan government said a plane carrying Zelensky was delayed at Chisinau airport on Tuesday after a Russian drone - reported to be jet-powered - entered Moldovan airspace.Earlier this year Ukraine showed relative success in countering Russian drones and was intercepting 94% of long-range drones, according to Zelensky. But the speed of the newer drones has prompted the latest round in Kyiv and Moscow's arms race. On 10 August, Ukraine's deputy head of military intelligence, Maj Gen Vadym Skibitskyi, said his forces needed new interceptor missiles "capable of matching [jet-drones'] speed".

schema.headline: Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches

title: Alice Kinsella: British gymnast continues historic comeback at international level
description: Olympic gymnast Alice Kinsella says "it's hard to put into words" how she feels about returning to international competition as her groundbreaking com
body: Olympic gymnast Alice Kinsella says "it's hard to put into words" how she feels about returning to international competition as her groundbreaking comeback to the sport continues this weekend.The two-time European champion became the first British artistic gymnast to resume elite competition after giving birth, when she finished fourth in the beam at the British Championships in March.Now the 25-year-old is preparing for her first competition back in Team GB colours at a senior team international against France, Switzerland, Germany and Italy at Fenton Manor in Stoke on 12-13 September."It's kind of crazy - it's such a surreal feeling but I am very excited," Kinsella told BBC Radio Stoke."It's only been a year, postpartum. Training-wise, it's been tough, but it's been good.  I'm excited to finally get out there. I'm ready, I'm doing everything I can to get back where I was."It's been a rollercoaster but a good one."Kinsella's pioneering journey back to the sport is so rare it became the subject of a university research paper into elite gymnasts resuming their careers after giving birth.Her son Parker, who was born in September 2025, is already a source of inspiration and he will be watching his mum compete at the weekend as Kinsella competes in all four pieces of apparatus - balance beam, bars, vault and floor - for the first time."It's really special because I've wanted to try to get back into a team and this is a really good start because it's a little four-way," Kinsella, who trains with Park Wrekin Gymnastics Club in Shropshire, said."It's not too big of a competition which is really good. I'm definitely nervous, but it's hard to put into words - it's been so long."I did the British [Championships] in March but only did beam and that's all I was training really but now I'm trying to do all four so it's more on the body."It's not like you've done one piece and you can stop thinking about everything, you've got to move on to the next and think about that. So it's been tough."After revealing she only took "three or four weeks off" after giving birth, Kinsella returned to training at the start of the year with the longer-term intention of being at the World Championships in China in 2027 and the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.But, after finding herself ahead of schedule so far this year, she wanted to take the chance to step it up."My main goal was to try to get back next year but I'm actually a lot further forward than I thought I would be," added Kinsella, who won bronze in the team event at the Tokyo Olympics in 2020."So that's why I'm doing this competition because I just want to get out there, compete, because I don't like doing nothing."What makes Kinsella's return so unique are the obvious challenges - and changes to the body - pregnancy and childbirth brings.There are many examples of women returning to the top of their sports after becoming mothers but gymnastics, where vital pelvic floor and core strength are both weakened during pregnancy, is different.Kinsella said her gymnastics background has played a big part in her being able to return to physical exercise so quickly but said she "didn't feel too bad" when she got back in the gym."I always had that goal to get back into the gym and I think when I've got a goal set I will do everything I can to achieve it," she said."Getting back into a leotard with how my body's changed just feels very weird but I guess that shows what my body has gone through and I try to think about it in a positive way."Her body is not the only thing that has changed with Kinsella adding that parenthood has helped her become better at taking the pressure off herself as an athlete."Having a baby changes your life - I'm very patient, whereas before Parker I was not patient at all," she said."When I made one tiny mistake I would get so annoyed, but now if I just make like a little mistake I'm totally fine about it."You have to be patient with kids, they're crazy. So I've definitely changed in that aspect but style-wise and gymnastics-wise like I don't think that's changed."Things are harder to get back and to do but I think the more I train it'll probably feel a lot easier."Kinsella said when she started her comeback "no one really had any idea what I was going to able to do" and wants to keep levels of expectation for her international return as realistic as possible.For her, this weekend in Stoke is there primarily "just to enjoy it" and to "get the experience of all four pieces [of apparatus] again"."My body's changed, I can't do the same amount of training I used to do but I'm definitely getting back to that," Kinsella said."We're definitely on the right track to be where I was before I had Parker. My goal was to start competing next year properly on all four. "It's going to be really fun. Whatever happens, happens, good, bad. I'm just proud I'm able to be back out there a year postpartum."

schema.headline: Alice Kinsella: British gymnast continues historic comeback at international level

title: Mikel Arteta close to signing new contract with Arsenal
description: The perception of Arsenal's transfer window varies depending on who you speak to - but there will be no disagreement from anyone at the Emirates Stadi
body: The perception of Arsenal's transfer window varies depending on who you speak to - but there will be no disagreement from anyone at the Emirates Stadium over how crucial their next expected signing will be.With the market closed until January, the club are now in the process of finalising an agreement with manager Mikel Arteta over his protracted new contract.Well-placed sources indicate those discussions have moved forward recently amid full confidence from those involved in talks that the Spaniard will renew.Indeed, Arteta moved unequivocally last month to remove any lingering doubt over his future: "Everybody feels comfortable that the timing of the contract is not going to be an issue because my will certainly is to be here and I'm very happy here."My feeling from the club is the same one. That's why everyone is doing things in a very organic way."Similarly, Arsenal's chief executive Richard Garlick has said it was merely a "matter of time" before Arteta's new long-term deal was confirmed.Arteta can expect to become one of the best paid managers in world football once his new contract is signed - Arsenal committed to significantly improving on his current deal, worth £10m a season plus an extra £5m upon Champions League qualification.For Arsenal supporters, the official announcement can't come soon enough, particularly given his current deal now has just nine months left to run.Since his appointment in December 2019, Arteta has transformed Arsenal from a club that had lost its Champions League status to one that won the Premier League for the first time in 22 years last season.They are overwhelming favourites to retain their domestic crown and are fancied to win their first-ever Champions League this season.With that success comes power. Like Arsene Wenger before him, Arteta is categorically the most influential figure, certainly from a football perspective, at the club.People will say that the manager or head coach should always be the most authoritative figure at any football club - the reality is that is rarely the case.Arteta's fingerprints are all over the club - and most importantly the squad. Nothing happens from a first-team perspective without his approval.When Arsenal tried to sign Julian Alvarez and Vinicius Jr last month, it was Arteta who was at the forefront of the club's charm offensive.With that in mind, the thought of removing Arteta from that dynamic, certainly for Arsenal's ownership, is the unthinkable.One day, Spain will come calling - and a return to his homeland may attract Arteta, although he knows he is unlikely to be afforded the same authority at either Real Madrid or Barcelona – clubs that are historically entrenched in internal politics – than he is now.But at this moment, the attraction for Arteta is with Arsenal.This is a squad that has flourished under Arteta's tutelage. The average age of the squad (26.2 years) is one of the oldest in the Premier League. It's a group at its peak and primed to build a legacy on.Beyond the new financial terms and into footballing ambition, Arsenal are buying into Arteta's vision.The summer arrivals of Bruno Guimaraes and Ezri Konsa were sizeable investments given both turn 30 next year, while the albeit failed pursuits of Vinicius Jr and Alvarez provided Arteta with evidence that the club's American owners are willing to spend heavily on elite talent.It's the sort of ambition Arteta is understood to have made clear he wanted to see as talks over his contract progressed.Arteta's six years at the Emirates already makes him the longest-serving manager in the Premier League and EFL by some distance - his new deal will take him closer to a decade in north London.Yet there appear to be no signs of Arteta taking his foot off the gas.

schema.headline: Mikel Arteta close to signing new contract with Arsenal

title: Air traffic chaos and compensation: 'Shutdown cost us more than £1,000'
description: Catie, 30, and Phil, 34, were sat on a British Airways flight to Ljubljana on Tuesday that never took off. If a flight is cancelled, airlines must get
body: Catie, 30, and Phil, 34, were sat on a British Airways flight to Ljubljana on Tuesday that never took off. If a flight is cancelled, airlines must get customers to their destination as quickly as possible at no extra cost, even if it is with a rival carrier.Alternatively, passengers can take a refund, which should also be offered for flight delays of more than five hours.In Catie and Phil's case, the alternative flight offered would not have arrived until Saturday morning - four days into their week-long holiday. So they took the refund. That was not easy. The chatbot only seemed to allow them to rebook, and it took more than an hour waiting to speak to BA on the phone before the refund was confirmed. It will take a week to be paid.When airlines are at fault, extra compensation is paid under UK and EU rules. But not this time, because the air traffic control issues were beyond airlines' control. Even so, airlines themselves are furious that they have been saddled with a bill of millions of pounds.BA also refunded the couple's car hire, which had been organised through the airline. The problem for the couple was that they had booked accommodation and excursions separately, and that is money they have lost.

schema.headline: Air traffic chaos and compensation: 'Shutdown cost us more than £1,000'

title: US Open 2026: Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff & Elena Rybakina make up historic semi-final line-up
description: "Oh, wow".That was Coco Gauff's surprised reaction when she learned she was part of a US Open semi-final line-up the like of which has not been seen i
body: "Oh, wow".That was Coco Gauff's surprised reaction when she learned she was part of a US Open semi-final line-up the like of which has not been seen in more than half a century.For the first time since 1975, the top four seeds in the women's singles draw have reached the semi-finals at the New York major.Now, 51 years later, the stars have aligned once again with Aryna Sabalenka, Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula and Gauff all surviving three-set thrillers to create a semi-final line-up for the ages."How amazing - it doesn't get much better than that does it?" former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live."It has felt fantastic the whole tournament - I just feel like I've been more enthused about looking forward to the match-ups this Grand Slam than any I can remember."It is the first time the top-four ranked players have reached the women's semi-finals at any Grand Slam since Wimbledon in 2009, and it hints at a shift away from the unpredictable landscape that has characterised the women's game in recent years.Since the start of 2020, there have been 13 different Grand Slam women's singles champions - compared to just seven on the men's side."I just feel like there's lots of really big names now, big personalities going up against each other and it's really exciting," Croft said."We've been blessed with the amount of intriguing matches we've had. You're seeing these warriors out on court."Top seed and two-time defending champion Sabalenka will face American Pegula in Thursday's first semi-final (00:00 BST, Friday), while Rybakina - who will replace Sabalenka as the new world number one on Monday - takes on fourth seed Gauff afterwards.While Sabalenka is bidding to become the first woman since Serena Williams in 2014 to win three successive US Open titles, Pegula is the only player remaining in the women's draw still chasing a maiden Grand Slam.The pair need no introduction to each other, having faced each other 13 times.That includes the past two US Open tournaments, when Sabalenka denied Pegula a first major title in the 2024 final and fought back to win in last year's semi-finals."It's fun to look at it like a rivalry. I think that's what motivates me," said Pegula."I know that she's definitely pushed me to become a better player, so I always respect and appreciate that aspect of our rivalry."Pegula, who has got the better of Sabalenka on four occasions on the WTA Tour, said beating the four-time major winner at Grand Slam level is a "hurdle" she must overcome.Sabalenka, meanwhile, said she was "super excited" to face Pegula, who arrived in New York in better form after reaching the final in both Washington and Cincinnati."I'm loving playing against her because it's a battle, because it's a fight, and I love being under pressure and going through tough challenges," said Sabalenka, who is into her first semi-final since falling to Pegula at June's Berlin Open.Pegula added of Sabalenka: "I know she hasn't maybe had the best results this summer, but I know that she has a lot of confidence playing here at this tournament, and she's going for a three-peat."By reaching the semi-finals, second seed Rybakina will become the new world number one on Monday - ending Sabalenka's 99-week reign at the top.But the second seed has described the top ranking as "just a number" and stressed that her focus remains focused on winning her third Grand Slam title."It's never quite the same if you become world number one having lost a Grand Slam final or semi-final just beforehand, so she will be trying to cap off an absolutely perfect couple of weeks by winning the title," tennis correspondent Russell Fuller said on BBC Radio 5 Live.Standing in her way, however, is Gauff, who will have the home crowd's backing on Arthur Ashe Stadium.The 22-year-old American, who won the Flushing Meadows title in 2023 but suffered fourth-round exits in the following two years, said she has a different perspective to this year's tournament."Sometimes you're just so focused on the now, now, now, because you want it now, and obviously you want to take advantage of your opportunities," she said."In the grand scheme of things, [I'm] definitely sitting here in a different mindset and perspective than I was last year."It inspires me a little bit more to keep working, as I see how much I have improved in a year."Gauff leads the head-to-head 2-1, but Australian Open champion Rybakina fought back from a set down to triumph in last month's Canadian Open semi-finals."I'm going to have some aces hit on me and some winners hit on me, but I'm going to keep fighting and give it my all. That's all I can do," Gauff said.

schema.headline: US Open 2026: Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff & Elena Rybakina make up historic semi-final line-up

title: August joint hottest month on record as climate change and El Niño drive heat
description: Dr Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus, described August as "a remarkable month in the global climate record", and its impacts
body: Dr Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus, described August as "a remarkable month in the global climate record", and its impacts had been "increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world".The combination of record air temperatures, record ocean heat and Europe's exceptional summer showed how climate change was now driving extremes across "both the atmosphere and the oceans", she said.World's oceans hit highest temperature on recordUN climate chief Simon Stiell said the record clearly showed humanity's impact on the climate."The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiralling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fuelling," he said.On top of the ongoing impact of the use of fossil fuels, the rise of a powerful El Niño is making matters worse, the researchers have said.El Niño is a natural climate pattern in which a band of the eastern Pacific turns unusually warm, releasing vast amounts of stored ocean heat into the atmosphere and nudging global temperatures upwards for around a year.The one currently being experienced is still strengthening and could become one of the most powerful on record, according to the Copernicus team.The biggest impact of this natural phenomenon on global temperatures is expected to hit over the coming year, meaning the current run of records may have further to go.

schema.headline: August joint hottest month on record as climate change and El Niño drive heat

title: The one thing you need to do to succeed - according to top bosses
description: Figure caption, Big bosses reveal the secret to getting hiredByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter What makes someone stand out in a crowded workplace?For so
body: Figure caption, Big bosses reveal the secret to getting hiredByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter What makes someone stand out in a crowded workplace?For some bosses, it's less about having the perfect CV and more about the way you think, the questions you ask and whether you're prepared to take a chance.Six business founders and leaders share the qualities they notice most and the advice they would give to people trying to get ahead.Don't limit yourselfImage source, Getty ImagesCharlotte Tilbury says one of the biggest things that has driven her career is refusing to let other people set limits on what she can do."Nothing is impossible in life - it's only your own limitations you give yourself."The beauty mogul says there will always be naysayers, and there were plenty of people who told her she was "mad" or that her ideas would not work but it's important to ignore them.Tilbury recommends trying not to think of setbacks as mistakes, but as opportunities to rethink and improve."I don't think about mistakes, I think mistakes are opportunities," she says.Many of the biggest challenges she faced ultimately made her a stronger business leader and "challenge is opportunity and it leads you to greater places".Fake confidenceCharlie Bowes-Lyon, co-founder of deodorant brand Wild, says attitude matters far more than having the perfect set of skills."For me, it's 90% attitude and 10% skills, as skills can be taught, attitude can't."One thing he wishes he had realised earlier is that even successful people do not always feel as confident as they appear and "everyone is faking it until they're making it". If you find yourself at a job interview, Bowes-Lyon says it's really important to have a few questions at the end as "candidates who say they have no questions rarely get the job".One question he recommends asking the interviewer is what success in the job looks like.Read more about how Charlie Bowes-Lyon runs WildBe curiousImage source, Marcia KilgoreMarcia Kilgore, the serial entrepreneur behind brands including Beauty Pie and Soap and Glory, says curiosity is one of the main qualities she looks for when hiring.She values people who will "roll their sleeves up, ask lots of questions and think about how they can be useful".Kilgore also says good communication is crucial as she realised early on in her career that a lack of communication is often the reason things break down.Her advice to communicate well in the workplace is to "listen to what's being asked and take a breath or five" before responding."Your response doesn't have to be immediate, but it does have to be considered."Read more about how Marcia Kilgore built her beauty brands.Say yes to everythingAnabel Kindersley, CEO and co-owner of Neal's Yard Remedies, says one of the best ways to build your skills is to keep saying yes to new opportunities."Do everything and say yes to everything - it might feel uncomfortable but do it anyway," she says.It is an approach that has shaped her own varied career, from working as a child actress to becoming an author and later moving into business.She adds that honesty really matters and you should be truthful about your experience and confident in what you can offer. When hiring, Kindersley says she looks for people with "equal EQ as IQ", valuing emotional intelligence alongside ability.Step outside your comfort zoneImage source, Charlie NunnCharlie Nunn, group chief executive of Lloyds Banking Group, says curiosity, resilience and an increasing willingness to think about how AI tools can also be used in the future are some of the skills he values most in his employees.He also really puts an emphasis on hiring people who are good at working in a team as "at the heart of most jobs is the ability to work together in support of something much bigger".His advice for building experience is to take on opportunities that are outside your comfort zone.Nunn says he was "terrified" about taking on retail roles earlier in his career, but found they gave him valuable experience."If something feels risky, try and do it as you'll learn more from it and it'll build breadth around your CV that you didn't have previously."Read about Charlie Nunn's top ways to manage your money. Use AI but don't rely on itJames Reed, chairman and chief executive of recruitment company Reed, says one of the biggest mistakes people make is thinking about what an employer can do for you rather than what you can offer in return."The biggest mistake is thinking that the world owes you a living," he says and instead suggests you should ask yourself: "How am I the solution to an employer?"As AI is increasingly used in recruitment, Reed says applicants need to think about how their skills are being picked up by technology as well as by a person."Try and mirror the job description with your skills and experiences in your application," he says, so that the match between what an employer is looking for and what you can offer is clear.He describes AI as "a wonderful tool", but says it should not replace your own judgement or voice – the aim is for it to strengthen an application rather than expect it to do the work for you.Read more about James Reed's advice on how to get a job.

schema.headline: The one thing you need to do to succeed - according to top bosses

title: RNLI reviews security after protests in Dover and Portsmouth
description: The RNLI is reviewing its security procedures to ensure the safety of its members after protests in Dover and Portsmouth which saw its members targete
body: The RNLI is reviewing its security procedures to ensure the safety of its members after protests in Dover and Portsmouth which saw its members targeted. As part of this, volunteers have been told to consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing in some circumstances while representing the charity. It comes after the charity helped carry around 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight, to Eastney, in Langstone Harbour, where roads were blocked by protesters. Following this, some crew members had their photos and names shared on social media, in posts accusing them of treason. RNLI chief executive Peter Sparkes called the abuse "wholly unacceptable in a civilised society".As a charity, the RNLI relies on donations from the public to fund its work.  Many lifeboat stations have shops attached to them, not just to raise money, but also to raise the profile of the organisation.  Volunteers have been told they are "empowered to make decisions to keep yourself, your team or crew safe" and "go home or close for the day if you need to".For it to tell its volunteers they should feel empowered to shut shops or even lifeboat stations if they do not feel safe shows how seriously it is taking potential issues. Sussex Police are looking to establish whether any criminal offences have been committed.  The Home Office said that platforms should enforce their own terms of service over this matter, and "take swift action against discriminatory content". In a statement to the BBC, a Home Office spokesperson said: "Directing abuse at people who risk their lives in the service of others is appalling." They added: "Where content is shared to intimidate, harass or incite violence against someone, that can cross into criminality," adding the Home Office would work "with platforms and law enforcement to ensure appropriate action is taken".Speaking to BBC Breakfast about the new safety guidance for RNLI volunteers, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "My concern is about people calling them traitors and accusing them of treason, that is quite wrong. "It is the government's job to stop the boats. They should not be attacking volunteers."In a message sent to volunteers, Sparkes said its participation in the rescue on Sunday had been requested by HM Coastguard. "This was the first time we have been involved in a Channel crossing incident of this magnitude this far west," he said. Initially crews from Bembridge and Yarmouth stations were involved, later being joined by crews from four more stations after "large numbers of protesters were in and near the water in Portsmouth". During the incident, the RNLI said it also helped to ensure the safety of anti-migrant protesters in the sea off Portsmouth.BBC Verify spoke to Neil, one of the volunteers who was called a "traitor" and whose image was shared online. "We were there, purely for the safety of the protesters in the water," he said."It would be nice for those people who called me a traitor to know that I'm not a traitor." Speaking to BBC Newsnight, RNLI vice-president Sir Robin Knox-Johnston encouraged people abusing lifeboat crews to "have some sense about this". Sir Robin, a legendary sailor who was the first man to sail solo non-stop around the world, said: "The people who are abusing the volunteers - I wonder how abusive they'd be if they suddenly got a stitch when they're out swimming? "They'd be screaming for the RNLI to rescue them and the RNLI would do it."In his message to volunteers, Peter Sparkes said "at times of increased media activity like this it is only natural that members of the public, supporters, family and friends may have questions about our lifesaving work in the Channel". "When our crews are tasked by HM Coastguard, we will go to the aid of those who need our assistance, including those crossing one of the world's busiest shipping lanes in small, overcrowded and unseaworthy boats," he said. "When called upon, we rescue people - men, women, and children - in distress."He said the RNLI would then pass over responsibility for the people it rescued to the ambulance service, HM Coastguard, police or Border Force. Figures from the RNLI show only a tiny fraction of its lifeboat launches involved assisting people "in distress in the Channel", with the majority of small boats intercepted by Border Force.  Sparkes encouraged crew members to take measures to ensure they feel safe in their roles. He said volunteers could do things like "choosing not to wear RNLI branded clothing when representing our charity in public places" or "removing yourself from a conversation with a member of public if you feel uncomfortable".  He also encouraged RNLI members to visibly wear ID identifying themselves while on site, and to challenge anyone not wearing an ID - especially if they are acting suspiciously or trying to gain access to the building.

schema.headline: RNLI reviews security after protests in Dover and Portsmouth

title: 'My cancer spread while I waited 128 days for an op':  The cost of England's care gap
description: Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year.The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up w
body: Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year.The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up waiting nearly five months, by which time the cancer had spread, making his surgery more complex."I was so frustrated and angry and couldn't understand why they would leave me like that," says Alan.On two occasions, scans were cancelled because machines had broken and for weeks he heard little or nothing from the hospital about when he would eventually have the urgent surgery.Alan is one of thousands each month in England who are not being treated within the target timeframe.Earlier this year, the government's National Cancer Plan, along with the NHS Planning Guidance, set out that 80% of patients in England would start treatment within 62 days from urgent GP referral by March 2027. This was to reach 85% by March 2029.But in the months since the government announced this ambition, performance has got worse, according to NHS England data, not better.Now, 71.2% of patients start cancer treatment within the 62 day timeframe. Previously it was 71.9%.Radiotherapy UK analysis, shared exclusively with the BBC, suggests more than 2,800 extra patients would need to start treatment every month - a near 15% increase on current numbers - to achieve the March 2027 target.That is likely to grow as referrals keep rising across nearly every cancer type.Price says thousands of patients "are going to die unnecessarily, just because the government can't get their act together to treat people on time".  For every month a cancer patient waits before starting treatment, their chance of survival falls by around 10%, on average.By the time Alan had his operation, the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes and the nodule "had grown at an alarming rate", according to the lung specialist.He has since been told the cancer has cleared awaiting his one-year review, but the operation has left him in debilitating pain. "I used to play golf and get out and about. Now I can't do any of the things I love," says Alan.Roughly 54,000 more patients will need to start treatment within 62 days before 2029 for the government to hit its goal.One NHS trust that is gaining traction on its waiting list numbers is Salisbury, but it is still not hitting targets.  Staff say there is no single fix, just a relentless focus on getting the basics right; making sure patients know about their appointments and turn up, keeping IT systems working, recruiting the right people, making sure surgical lists are full and expanding capacity.Much of the visible progress has come through skin and prostate cancer, two of the most common cancers in the country.But staff in Salisbury also say missed appointments, whether down to late letters, illness, transport problems or anxiety, are a constant drain on a system already stretched thin.Emilia Scutt, cancer manager in Salisbury, says that efforts to reduce missed appointments have really helped their numbers."We know cancer can be terrifying so we are a bit like a dog with the bone, backing up patients and supporting them wherever we can."Trusts with the sharpest declines in performance - including Buckinghamshire Healthcare, Bolton NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust, East Cheshire, and Torbay and South Devon - told the BBC they face pressures across the board. Rising demand, workforce shortages and diagnostic bottlenecks have all played a part.Some pointed to industrial action and staff sickness, others to reliance on outside diagnostic providers or major changes to how their systems work. All say they are investing in extra capacity, working through backlogs and redesigning pathways, and are already seeing early signs of improvement."If government is serious about delivering on the ambitions of the National Cancer Plan for England, it must match ambition with urgency," said Steve Haines of Macmillan Cancer Support.He said that "visible progress" was needed on a promise to set up a National Cancer Board to oversee progress on improving waiting times and treatment.A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson says the National Cancer Plan "will help more people get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner".They concedes that "there is more to do, but we are determined to return cancer performance to the standards people rightly expect".Additional reporting Daniel Wainwright and Jess Carr

title: Wrexham couple spent £23,000 on fertility treatment but now embryos will be destroyed
description: Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nat (left) and Nik Fraser-Edwards went through six rounds of failed artificial insemination before they
body: Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nat (left) and Nik Fraser-Edwards went through six rounds of failed artificial insemination before they were successful through a different type of fertility treatmentByAlexandra BánfiBBC WalesUpdated 1 hour agoNat and Nik Fraser-Edwards celebrated their son Jude's first birthday last month.After rounds of failed fertility treatment, Jude was a dream come true for the couple who said they hoped to give him a brother or sister next year. But now their dreams have come "crashing down".Their sperm donor has withdrawn his consent for further use, and the remaining five embryos in storage will be destroyed after paying £23,000 on fertility treatment.In the UK, a sperm or egg donor can withdraw consent up until the embryo is transferred into the womb.The couple now want the law changed so that once an embryo has been created, consent cannot be withdrawn.Figure caption, Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards spent £23,000 on fertility treatment but now their embryos will be destroyedThe UK government said it sympathised and added it is "keeping all aspects of the regulatory regime under review".When they returned from their honeymoon in 2023, the couple from north Wales started fertility treatment.They took out loans and went through rounds of failed artificial insemination in a journey that cost them a total of £23,000."There was a lot of pain during that time, and everyone around us seemed to be getting pregnant," recalled Nat, 37."All you see is babies. It's not just wanting that baby so much, it's the cancelled plans in case you get that smiley face."It was only when they turned to a different type of treatment, called ICSI , where the egg is fertilised with sperm and the embryo is created outside of the body, that they had success.Nat and Nik ended up with six embryos and in August last year, Jude was born.Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Jude was born last August and Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards (left to right) were hoping to get pregnant with their second child in January next yearThe embryos were put into storage until the couple were ready to grow their family. It was during a telephone consultation in June that they found out their embryos would be destroyed."It was very much, 'unfortunately your donor has withdrawn his consent to use your embryos'," said Nat, who lives in Penyffordd, near Wrexham."They said, 'we keep them for a cooling off period of a year and' - I think the hardest word for us was - 'we then allow them to perish'."We were absolutely floored."Nik said the couple felt "blindsided" by the fact that their sperm donor could withdraw consent at that stage."Yes, we'd signed something," she added. "But we didn't ever recall it being verbally said."Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards (left to right) recently celebrated Jude's first birthday after going through rounds of failed fertility treatmentThe number of donors in the UK that withdraw consent is unknown as the data isn't collected. While it is rare, it is not unheard of.Sam Beesley and Carly Estlick are expecting their first child, a boy they plan to call Finn, in October after going through IVF."I've been someone who knew from a young age that my job in life was to be a mother," said Sam, 41.Just like Nat and Nik, Sam and Carly were told last month that their sperm donor had withdrawn consent and their 10 remaining embryos will be destroyed next year.Image source, Sam BeesleyImage caption, Sam Beesley and Carly Estlick are expecting their first child Finn in October this year"When we got the letter saying he had withdrawn consent, it felt like the wind was taken out of our sails," said Sam from Shrewsbury."We had been so focussed on the pregnancy and something going wrong, I don't think it's really sunk in yet."Carly is already grieving. In her head, they've already been destroyed. Whereas until that day in 2027, I will not stop fighting."Sam said the news has put pressure on their current pregnancy."Carly is very fearful that something will happen to Finn," she said. "It has crossed my mind.The couple who were told their embryos will be destroyedThe BBC speak to Natalie and Nicola Fraser-Edwards who spent £23,000 on fertility treatment. But now their sperm donor has withdrawn consent so they can't use the remaining embryosListen now on BBC Sounds"I did have some reduced movements the other day and had to go to hospital. You can't help thinking, is this going to be ripped away from us as well?"This is probably our only shot at being parents. I don't know how we could afford to go through it again financially, emotionally, physically."For both couples, fertility treatment has had an emotional and financial impact.Nat and Nik say they would have paid anything to have a family, but that the total £23,000 bill means that they did have to make "sacrifices"."We lived on the breadline for quite a while, just to make this work," Nat said. "Taking out a loan in order to pay the excessive bill."Image source, Sam BeesleyImage caption, Sam Beesley and Carly Estlick have said they're facing the same fate as Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards as they've been told their embryos will be destroyed in August 2027 Nat and Nik also say they can't afford to go through treatment again, and, for Nik, this means she may never get to experience pregnancy."I think, as a woman, it's an amazing thing to be able to do and I didn't want to have any regrets later in life," said Nik, 36."We knew we were going to have a sibling for Jude. I think the tables turned a little bit watching Nat go through that experience and I was thinking, 'yeah I'd love to do that'."The UK fertility regulator HFEA has said that any change in the law on sperm donation is down to the UK government."It's about each person who provides an egg or sperm having that autonomy to consent and make that decision to whether they're happy for a child to be born in treatment," said Rachel Cutting, HFEA's director of compliance.Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nik said watching Nat carry Jude made her realise she wanted to experience pregnancy as well"Once the embryos in the uterus, in the woman's womb, there can't be a withdrawal of consent for that."The way that the law is written is that consent can be withdrawn from up to that point."We can look at it further, but it is for the law to be changed and that's not something within the power that the HFEA has. We can't change the law. But we are sympathetic to cases like this."The HFEA has said it is important that clinics warn patients of the possibility of donors withdrawing consent "because it is really upsetting and distressing when this happens".The UK government said it also sympathises with "anyone facing difficult and distressing circumstances during fertility treatment."A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "We continue to work closely with the fertility sector to support high-quality, compassionate care, and we keep all aspects of the regulatory regime under review to the same end."If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

title: Funeral for PC Clough killed in Middlesbrough A66 crash
description: Police and army mourn officer killed in crashImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Hundreds of police officers, emergency service workers and army vete
body: Police and army mourn officer killed in crashImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Hundreds of police officers, emergency service workers and army veterans attended PC Tom Clough's funeralByClaudia Robinsonin Redcar and Evie LakeNorth East and CumbriaUpdated 32 minutes agoPolice officers and army veterans have gathered for the funeral of the second officer killed in a head-on crash.PC Tom Clough, 38, died on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 22 August alongside his colleague PC Matthew Blades when a Volkswagen Passat hit their marked police car. Five young men in the Passat also died.Members of the public also gathered at Kirkleatham Walled Gardens, in Redcar, for the funeral, along with family, friends and former colleagues from the Civil Nuclear Constabulary in Sellafield, Cumbria.Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said PC Clough's partner had said public support "brought them so much strength".The ceremonial procession made its way along Plantation Road towards the Walled Gardens, accompanied by the music of a lone piper.The road was lined on both sides with standard bearers who had lowered their flags before the cortege went past.At its head was a mounted police unit of four horses.Immediately behind them came the hearse carrying PC Clough's coffin, draped with the Union Flag and topped with his custodian helmet.The hearse was flanked by officers in ceremonial dress escorting the coffin to the service.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, PC Tom Clough died while on duty on the A66 near Middlesbrough on 22 AugustImage source, PA MediaImage caption, A mounted police unit led the cortegePC Clough had served in the British Army from 2006 to 2012 and was a lance corporal with the Royal Logistics Corps.His last unit was 11 Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Search Regiment.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Uniformed officers lined Plantation Road as PC Clough's coffin drove pastOfficers had been pursuing the Passat seconds before it collided with PC Blades and PC Clough's car on the dual carriageway.The pair had been looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered an automated number plate recognition camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit, according to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.The Passat's occupants - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, PC Clough's family said they were grateful for the public supportAfter he left the Army, PC Clough joined the Civil Nuclear Constabulary and worked at Sellafield, in Cumbria, then served with British Transport Police and finally joined Cleveland Police, where he was an armed response officer.Somerville said she had "the privilege" of speaking to his partner."The family are grateful for all of the support from the public, it's brought them so much strength," she said."She wants people to know that Tom wasn't just a police officer, he was a partner and a brother and a son and most importantly a father to a sausage dog called Frank, who was the love of his life."More than £1.2m was raised to help the families of PC Blades and PC Clough, a fundraiser which was set up by Cleveland Police Federation."Tom used to say that he didn't think anybody would come to his funeral and he was wrong," Somerville said."He was so wrong."He was described as giving his everything to everybody."Additional reporting by PA Media.Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Tees on BBC Sounds. title: Should Chelsea be stripped of 2016-17 title and Tottenham crowned champions?
description: Should Tottenham be retrospectively crowned Premier League champions for the 2016-17 season?That's the opinion of former manager Mauricio Pochettino,
body: Should Tottenham be retrospectively crowned Premier League champions for the 2016-17 season?That's the opinion of former manager Mauricio Pochettino, who led Spurs to a second-place finish - seven points behind Chelsea - that season.This is about Chelsea making £47m in secret payments, according to a Premier League investigation, to unregistered agents and third parties to seal transfers between 2011 and 2018.The transfers included Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o, Willian, Ramires, David Luiz, Andre Schurrle and Nemanja Matic.Four of those - Hazard, Willian, Luiz and Matic - were at the club in 2016-17.During that period Chelsea won two Premier League titles (2014-15 and 2016-17), two FA Cups (2011-12 and 2017-18), the EFL Cup (2014-15) and the Europa League (2018–19).Chelsea have been fined by Uefa, the Premier League and the Football Association, but Pochettino thinks that is not enough."If they admitted they broke the rules, the Premier League title was for the second-best team," Pochettino said.Pochettino is one of the first people of significance to articulate what many feel - that Chelsea got off lightly with a fine.Fans of Everton and Nottingham Forest have pointed out that their clubs faced points deductions for relatively small profit and sustainability breaches, while Chelsea sought to sign star players with secret payments.Meanwhile, there is no sign of a verdict in the case of Manchester City's 115 charges for alleged breaches of Premier League financial rules.Does Pochettino have a point? And how much of an impact did those four players have on the title race?Hazard is seen as the poster boy for Chelsea's breaches.The Blues fought off most of Europe's top clubs to sign him from Lille for £32m in the summer of 2012.Between May 2013 and August 2016, according to the investigation, seven payments totalling £5.6m were made to an unregistered agent "for the benefit of the club in connection with Hazard's transfer".Pochettino's argument is that Spurs could have beaten other clubs to the signing of players of similar ability had they also ignored the rules.What about Hazard's impact in the 2016-17 season?It was considerable.The Belgium forward started 36 Premier League games, scored 16 goals and provided five assists. Only Cesar Azpilicueta started more matches, and only Diego Costa netted more goals (20).Hazard was Chelsea's player of the year, was named in the Professional Footballers' Association (PFA) team of the year, and made the shortlist for PFA player of the year.Then there's the direct impact of his goals and assists in the results of four fixtures.Hazard scored the first goal in a 2-1 win over West Ham in August, then scored a goal and provided an assist in a 2-0 victory over Southampton in November.In March he scored the opener as Chelsea again beat the Hammers 2-1, and got both goals in a 2-0 win over Manchester City in April.You could argue that input was worth 10 points.There is no doubt that Hazard had a huge influence, but this was his fifth season at the club. It was not as if Chelsea signed him in the summer of 2016.The investigation found that Chelsea made payments totalling £5.1m between 2012 and 2015 "to provide talent identification services in certain European countries".This was identified as payments in relation to the registrations of Ramires, Luiz, Schurrle and Matic.However, by 2016-17 Matic and Luiz were in their second spells at Chelsea. The deal with Benfica which meant Matic and Luiz swapped clubs in 2011 was looked into. Matic returned to Stamford Bridge in 2014, with Luiz having a spell at Paris St-Germain from 2014 to 2016.While the deals that took the players back to Chelsea were not specifically referenced, the association was created.Matic played 35 league games in 2016-17, including 30 in the starting XI. He scored one goal and set up seven.Only one of those attacking contributions influenced a result, but that was an assist for Chelsea's first goal in a 2-1 win over Tottenham in November.Luiz, who was named in the PFA team of the season, started 33 matches and scored one goal - the opener in a 1-1 draw at Liverpool in January.Tottenham were relentless at the end of the 2016-17 season, winning 12 of their final 13 matches to finish on 86 points.Yet Antonio Conte's Chelsea were almost as relentless, winning 11 of their last 13 to take the title with 93 points.Spurs' tally would have been enough for the title in 2015-16, when Leicester finished on 81.However, since 1999-2000, when Manchester United were champions on 79 points, 86 points would only have won the title twice, including the two most recent seasons.Tottenham's problem in 2016-17 was too many draws at the start of the campaign. Despite an unbeaten 11-game start, only five of those were victories.Chelsea lost more matches - five to Spurs' four - but secured 30 wins to Tottenham's 26.Pochettino might argue that the attacking influence from Willian and Hazard proved the difference, with those two players having attacking contributions in eight different matches which led to points.Then there is the mere aspect of sporting advantage - how the signings of players like Hazard enabled Chelsea to win trophies, qualify for the Champions League and therefore attract more top talent.Pochettino feels he should have a Premier League title to his name.Remember that he managed Chelsea for one season, when he struggled to win over supporters.Chelsea finished sixth in 2023-24, but neither Pochettino nor the club are likely to look back fondly on that period.It is different at Tottenham, with the Argentine still adored for his five-year spell in charge from 2014.As well as finishing as Premier League runners-up, he took the club to the Champions League final in 2018-19.The 86 points earned in 2016-17 is a club record too.So do Spurs fans share his view?"Of course I do," said Chris Paouros, co-founder and co-chair of Proud Lilywhites, external and Women of The Lane., external"He could tell me the moon was made of halloumi and I'd nod along."The Spurs 2016-17 team was the best in the league by most measures: best attack, best defence, fewest defeats, unbeaten at home in the last season of the old White Hart Lane."If the playing field was tilted, the least you can do is ask the question."Paouros knows Spurs will not be handed the title, but said the "rules have to mean something, whoever benefits".There is another side to this, however.If you get given a title a decade later because of a rule breach, could you celebrate it?"It would still be something that Spurs fans would celebrate," said Tristan Foot, secretary of the Tottenham Hotspur Supporters' Trust. "A victory over Chelsea, albeit 10 years after the event."But that sense of injustice is still there for other Premier League clubs."It means that to an extent crime does pay in football," Foot said. "And that's the serious underlying part all of this."During the transfer window they were signing players that we had no chance of winning, the obvious example being Willian."The Premier League has got to be better about imposing sporting sanctions and making sure that its rules actually have teeth."With all investigations now concluded, it seems unlikely that Pochettino - or anyone else - will get a retrospective trophy parade.Will clubs get that same feeling when the Manchester City saga is finally over?

title: Harry Styles extends tour, with Kylie as a support act
description: Image source, Anthony PhanImage caption, Harry Styles set a new world record with his residency at Wembley Stadium this summerByMusic correspondentHar
body: Image source, Anthony PhanImage caption, Harry Styles set a new world record with his residency at Wembley Stadium this summerByMusic correspondentHarry Styles is extending his record-breaking Together, Together tour in 2027, with 25 more shows, including a return to Wembley Stadium next August.The singer, who is currently in the middle of a 30-show residency at New York's Madison Square Garden, is adding dates in Ireland, Spain, Italy, Germany and France - who all missed out on the tour's first leg this summer.Every city will see a different support act, with 80s pop icons Tears For Fears playing at Wembley, and pop legend Kylie Minogue on the bill in Los Angeles.Although Minogue is a festival headliner in Europe, these shows will represent her first ever stadium concerts in the US.She celebrated the announcement on her Instagram stories, writing: "Together, together. Harry. Me. Can't wait to see you in April, LA."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The tour opened in Amsterdam in MayUnlike the first half of the tour, which concentrated on long residencies in cities like London and New York, the 2027 dates represent a more traditional rolling stage show.Styles will also play US stadiums for the first time as a solo artist - with dates booked in Phoenix, Dallas, Atlanta and Chicago.After confusion and outcry over ticket prices for the 2026 shows, the singer's team have made the pricing structure clear for his upcoming dates, specifying that prices will range from $60 to $300 (£44 to £221). The 2027 dates will also introduce "Unpredictable Fun Tickets," an initiative to make concerts more accessible to people on a limited income. The programme will make a limited number of tickets available for £20 in the UK, $20 in the US and €20 in Europe. Details on availability and how to apply will be announced soon. The cost of regular tickets will vary by city. Details, including on-sale dates, are available on the star's website., externalImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Almost one million people attended the Wembley shows, travelling from all over the world to see the former One Direction starFans were already aware that a second leg of Styles' tour was on the way, after the 32-year-old posted a note on Wednesday teasing what he called the "final" shows of the hugely-successful run."When we decided to do the 2026 tour I knew it would be special but what you turned it into was far beyond what I could have imagined," he wrote."I love playing music, I love being with all of you and being a part of the love and joy you all create together every night. That's why I wanted you to be the first to know we will be adding 2027 dates, which honestly, at first I found daunting."Being an artist is the only life I've ever known really, I have been doing this since I was 16 years old, and I feel like the luckiest person in the world to still be sharing these moments with you."Tomorrow's announcement will be the final cities of Together, Together," he continued. "After that, I don't know what comes next for me, but I know that I'm excited to find out."Image source, Anthony PhamImage caption, The singer is donating money from his UK shows to support grassroots venues

schema.headline: Harry Styles extends tour, with Kylie as a support act
